Most "the sound isn't working" moments are cables: the wrong one, the wrong socket, or one that's broken. Learn the
connectors, the two kinds of signal level, and how to coil a cable so it lasts.

## The connectors

- **1/4" (6.35 mm) jack**, two kinds that look almost the same:
  - **TS** (tip, sleeve: one black ring): **unbalanced**. Guitar and instrument cables. Also speaker cables for
    some amps, which are a different, thicker cable: **never** use a guitar cable between an amp head and a cabinet.
  - **TRS** (tip, ring, sleeve: two rings): **balanced** mono (keyboards to a mixer, studio monitors) or **stereo**
    (headphones, insert cables).
- **XLR**: three pins, locks in place. Microphones, balanced line outputs, DI to mixer. Male end points toward the
  mixer (the signal flows out of the pins).
- **3.5 mm mini jack**: phones, laptops, small headphones.
- **RCA (phono)**: home audio, DJ gear, older keyboards.
- **speakON**: locking speaker connector for PA speakers and amp cabs; can't be confused with a signal cable.
- **MIDI** (5-pin DIN) and **USB** (A, B, C, Micro): control data, not audio (except USB audio interfaces).
- **IEC / kettle lead**: the detachable power cable on most gear.

## Balanced and unbalanced

An **unbalanced** cable has a signal wire and a shield. It picks up hum and noise, and longer than about 5–6 m
(guitar cables) it also loses treble.

A **balanced** cable carries the signal twice, once upside down. Any noise picked up along the way is the same on
both, and the input flips one and adds them, so the noise cancels. Balanced lines can run 50 m or more.

Both ends must be balanced to get the benefit: TRS to TRS, XLR to XLR, or TRS to XLR.

```{=html}
<div class="gear-fig" data-fig="balanced"></div>
```

## Levels: mic, instrument, line, speaker

| Level | Example | Goes into |
|---|---|---|
| **Mic** | microphones (very quiet) | mic input (XLR), with preamp gain |
| **Instrument (Hi-Z)** | electric guitar, bass pickups | instrument input, "Hi-Z" or "Inst" switch, or a **DI** |
| **Line** | keyboards, phones, mixers, interfaces | line input |
| **Speaker** | amplifier output to a passive speaker | only a speaker. Never into anything else |

A **DI box** turns an instrument or line signal into a balanced mic-level signal for a long run to the mixer. Use
one for bass, acoustic guitar with a pickup, and keyboards on stage.

## Signal flow

Follow the signal from the source to your ears: **instrument → cable → (pedals) → amp or DI → mixer → amplifier →
speakers**. When there's no sound, check each step in order: is it on, is the volume up, is the cable in the right
socket, does a different cable fix it, is the channel muted. Most problems are found in the first three.

```{=html}
<div class="gear-fig" data-fig="signal-flow"></div>
```

## Coil it right: over-under

Wrapping a cable round your elbow twists it; twisted cables kink and break inside. Use **over-under**: one loop
coiled normally, the next with a twist the other way. The cable lies flat, and thrown out it uncoils with no knots.
Close it with a velcro tie.

## Care and spares

- Pull by the **plug**, never the cable.
- Don't walk on, roll over, or bend cables sharply at the plug.
- Mark broken cables (tape: "BAD") and take them out of the box; don't coil them back in.
- Gig bag spares: two instrument cables, two XLRs, a patch cable, a 3.5 mm-to-two-1/4" lead, a DI, and spare batteries.
